(Today through Monday)...
Issued at 252 AM EDT Tue Sep 8 2026

After a couple days with more seasonable temperatures...warmer air 
will return to the Ohio Valley as ridging aloft once again expands 
back into the region through midweek. The ridge will flatten on 
Wednesday in response to a sharp upper trough traversing through 
southern Canada. This will enable a frontal boundary to drift into 
the area late Wednesday with chances for rain and thunderstorms into 
Thursday as it shifts slowly south. Dry and seasonable conditions 
return for late week but waves aloft riding within a largely zonal 
flow will contribute to isolated to scattered convection this 
weekend into next week.

Today through Thursday

Quiet early morning as the region remains under the influence of 
high pressure. Cirrus was spilling overtop of the upper level ridge 
centered to our west. 06Z temperatures were generally in the 60s.

The center of the aforementioned high will shift south through the 
Mid Atlantic region resulting in return flow advecting warmer and 
progressively more humid air into the Ohio Valley by Wednesday. The 
expansion of the ridge currently centered over the southern Plains 
will commence today with low level thermals supportive of highs 
returning to a range from the upper 80s in the northeast to the mid 
90s in the lower Wabash Valley. Higher dewpoint air will lag the 
temp rises and overall humidity levels this afternoon during peak 
heating will be manageable keeping peak heat indices in the lower 
and mid 90s. The onset of S/SW winds will aid in diurnal cu 
formation by midday particularly in the vicinity of a subtle 
inverted trough that will wash out this morning across the southeast 
half of the forecast area.  

More humid air will advect into the region tonight and especially 
Wednesday setting the stage for the hottest day of the week. The 
approach of a cold front from the north may produce a compressional 
heating component that could enable temperatures to overproduce on 
Wednesday. The wild card will be whether any remnants of convection 
or associated clouds over the upper Mississippi Valley late tonight 
and early Wednesday can make it into the forecast area by midday 
Wednesday and disrupt expected heating. Thermal profiles do support 
low to mid 90s for highs and the increase in humidity suggest heat 
indices will rise into the upper 90s and lower 100s during the 
afternoon. 

Scattered convection will be possible as the afternoon progresses 
Wednesday but expect more coverage by the evening as the boundary 
slides into the area and interacts with an axis of greater 
instability bisecting the forecast area from southwest to northeast. 
Initial convection Wednesday evening will carry a risk for damaging 
winds in the strongest cells with modest DCAPE values at 800-1000 
j/kg. A lack of BL shear along the boundary however will likely 
force a more pulse intensity convective profile before storms settle 
into a subsevere state Wednesday night with the focus shifting more 
to heavy rain and localized flooding. The frontal boundary will slow 
as it becomes near parallel to the upper flow through the night and 
into Thursday with the potential for storms to traverse across the 
same areas along and south of the I-70 corridor. With PWATs peaking 
near 2 inches...locally heavy rainfall will be possible until the 
front can shift south of the area Thursday night. 1 to 2 inches is 
possible with locally higher amounts between Wednesday afternoon and 
late Thursday.

Thursday Night through Monday

The cold front will shift south of the area Thursday night before 
gradually washing out across the Tennessee Valley on Friday as the 
boundary runs into the ridge over the southeast states. Weak high 
pressure will track through the Great Lakes for late week with dry 
and cooler conditions across central Indiana. Highs on Friday will 
be in the upper 70s and lower 80s.

As the high shifts into New England by early Saturday...return flow 
will draw the remnant moisture from the aforementioned front back 
north into the region in advance of a secondary boundary over the 
Upper Midwest. Forcing aloft is not overly impressive but the influx 
of moisture and instability into the region will likely be enough to 
generate isolated to scattered convection on both Saturday and 
Sunday. Developing low pressure over the High Plains early next week 
will shift a warm front into the lower Great Lakes and enable highs 
to again rise into the mid and upper 80s. Scattered convection is 
possible on Monday as well with more widespread rain and storms 
expected by Tuesday as the low tracks into the region.
